sections.h2: Selling a house in Evesham Township
sections.html:
Evesham Township is a large Burlington County suburb in South Jersey. A quick sale there comes down to three things: a resale certificate through the fire department, permits for any past work, and the state paperwork filed with the deed.

The township covers about 29 square miles and counted 46,826 people in 2020. The 2025 estimate is 49,525, which makes it the most populous municipality in the county. Many people say Marlton when they mean Evesham. Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it, so use both names when you describe the house.

Part of the township sits inside the Pinelands Area, a state-designated zone with its own land use rules. If your lot is near the wooded edge of town, check the zoning map before you describe the property to a buyer, since the rules can limit what a purchaser adds or builds later.

sections.h2: Home values and who owns them
sections.html:
Evesham is mostly owner-occupied, and values run above the national median. Figures below are 2020 to 2024 estimates.

About 89 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is modest and a listing that sits unsold tends to stand out. A price near the township median lands in the higher state fee band described under closing costs.

sections.h2: Roads and transit buyers ask about
sections.html:
Route 70 and Route 73 define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 crosses the northern part of Evesham from east to west, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two. A grade-separated interchange replaced the old Marlton Circle in 2011, and commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill became more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.

Resale certificate requests go to the Evesham Township Fire Department. Its site, eveshamfire.org, posts inspection scheduling and fees. Start that request early so the certificate is ready when the closing date arrives.

Permits are handled by the Community Development office in the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton, Room 204, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The construction office is at 856-983-2914, then option 4. A construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • Sheds and fences need a zoning permit, and a fence around a pool also needs a building permit meeting the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • Flood zone questions can be checked on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and the township mapping portal.

If a past owner finished a basement, deck or pool without paperwork, sort that out before you list. A buyer's attorney will ask for permit history, and a gap can stall a sale for weeks.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or short-term rental
sections.html:
You can sell a rental house, but the registration and fire inspection records go with the property, so gather them first. Evesham treats short-term rentals such as Airbnb and Vrbo listings like long-term rentals. They must pass a fire department inspection and register with the Township Clerk's Office.

Each time a new tenant moves in, the township requires a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm, and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance under N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3. A violation carries a $500 penalty, and the fire department sets the inspection fees.

If tenants live in the house, a buyer will want the lease, the deposit amount and the last inspection certificate. A cash purchaser who wants the house empty should say so in writing before the contract is signed, so notice periods can be planned. For landlord and tenant disputes, residents are pointed to the Burlington County court system and Legal Services of New Jersey.

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee and signs a Gross Income Tax residency form. Both are filed with the deed at the Burlington County Clerk. The fee is charged per $500 of the price written in the deed. For a standard sale over $350,000, the band from $200,000 to $550,000 is $4.80 per $500, and a price near Evesham's median home value falls in that band.

Homes sold above $1 million add a graduated percent fee that the seller owes, starting at 1 percent of the total price. Most Evesham sales fall well under that line.

Most New Jersey residents use the GIT/REP-3. Any GIT/REP form signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the current version, and older versions are rejected at recording. Questions go to the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275. Nonresident sellers owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

The county clerk also runs a free Property Fraud Alert system that alerts owners when a document is recorded in their name. It is worth joining before and after a sale.

sections.h2: How a fast as-is sale moves
sections.html:
A fast sale follows a short sequence, and each step has a clear owner. The steps assume you have clear title and no open permits.

  • Gather the deed, the last tax bill, any rental registration and your mortgage payoff figure.
  • Request the fire department resale certificate and fix anything it flags, or agree in the contract who fixes it.
  • Have your closing attorney order the title search and prepare the deed with the transfer fee and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over keys, and let the attorney record the deed with the Burlington County Clerk.

Cash buyers often agree to take a house in its current condition, which removes repair negotiations but not the certificate or the state filings. Title searches on older parcels can also turn up easements or old liens that the closing attorney has to clear before the deed records. Ask any buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays for each inspection in one written document before you commit.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?
faqs.a: Yes. Residential resales go through the Evesham Township Fire Department for a certificate, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Ask for the inspection date as soon as you decide to sell.

faqs.q: What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?
faqs.a: A buyer's attorney will likely require it to be resolved before closing, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. Call the construction office at 856-983-2914, option 4, to learn what a retroactive permit needs.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The state charges it when the deed is recorded with the Burlington County Clerk, based on the price in the deed, and an extra graduated fee applies above $1 million. Your closing attorney or title company will work out the exact figure.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. A nonresident seller files a GIT/REP form and pays an estimated Gross Income Tax of at least 2 percent of the price at closing unless an exemption on the form applies. The payment can be claimed back against the final tax owed when you file.

faqs.q: Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?
faqs.a: Yes. A portion of the township lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area, and the township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered. Check your parcel before marketing the property.
